biopower: Biopower is Michel Foucault's term for a modern form of power that manages whole populations and individual bodies through statistics, medicine, public health, and institutions, rather than simply commanding by law or force. On this view, states decide who is fostered and who is exposed to death, and surveillance leads people to police themselves.
category-mistake: A category mistake is the error of treating something as belonging to the wrong logical category—like saying a person 'consists of tallness' or asking what color Wednesday is. The idea comes from Gilbert Ryle, who argued Descartes made one by treating the mind as an invisible substance alongside the body.
cicero-duty: In On Duties (De Officiis), Cicero argued that moral duty governs every arena of life, including war and politics: even enemies must be treated as human beings, honor must never be traded for expedience, and conflict has rules. His book became a foundation of the Western just-war tradition.
dirty-hands: The problem of dirty hands, named after Jean-Paul Sartre's play and developed by Michael Walzer, asks what happens when a political leader must do something morally wrong—a lie, a betrayal, even killing—because the situation genuinely demands it. Many hold such acts can be necessary yet still wrong, leaving the leader a guilt that matters.
epistemic-injustice: Epistemic injustice, named by Miranda Fricker, is a wrong done to someone in their capacity as a knower. Testimonial injustice occurs when listeners discount what a person says because of prejudice about who they are; hermeneutical injustice occurs when a group lacks the shared concepts needed to make sense of its own experience.
ethics-of-lying: The ethics of lying and deception asks when, if ever, it is wrong to deceive. Kant famously held that lying is always wrong, however well-intentioned; utilitarians judge each lie by its consequences; and philosophers like Sissela Bok start from a strong presumption against lying, since deception robs others of informed choice and corrodes trust.
feminine-mystique: The 'feminine mystique' is Betty Friedan's name for the mid-century ideal that fulfilled housewifery and motherhood should satisfy educated American women—an ideal she called 'the problem that has no name,' whose unspoken misery helped launch 1960s feminism. Critics note Friedan mainly described white, middle-class women, a limitation later feminists have pressed.
gadamer-hermeneutics: Philosophical hermeneutics, developed by Hans-Georg Gadamer, holds that understanding is never a neutral transfer of fixed meaning: interpreters always approach a text or event from their own historical 'horizon' of assumptions, and understanding happens as a 'fusion of horizons' in which both interpreter and interpreted are changed. There is no view from nowhere.
jung-archetypes: For Carl Jung, archetypes are universal patterns—figures like the Hero, the Mother, and the Shadow—recurring in myths, religions, and dreams across cultures. On his view they arise from a collective unconscious, and stories grip us partly because they enact these primordial patterns; his psychology remains influential though scientifically contested.
jung-collective-unconscious: The collective unconscious is Carl Jung's controversial idea that beneath each person's individual unconscious lies a deeper, shared layer storing archetypes—primordial images and themes that surface in myths and dreams everywhere. Jung pointed to recurring symbols across unrelated cultures as evidence; many psychologists remain skeptical of the hypothesis.
jung-shadow: In Jungian psychology, the Shadow is the part of ourselves we refuse to acknowledge—the fears, desires, and traits our conscious identity disowns. Jung held these repressed contents still act on us, often projected onto others as monsters or enemies, and that real self-knowledge requires facing and integrating the Shadow rather than fleeing it.
korsgaard-constructivism: Christine Korsgaard's Kantian constructivism holds that moral obligations are not discovered like facts but constructed by us: in stepping back to reflect and choosing how to act, each person must legislate reasons they can endorse, and consistent self-government obligates them to value other people's humanity as their own. Morality is the law of a self we make.
lacan-mirror-stage: The mirror stage is Jacques Lacan's account of how an infant, seeing its mirror image, first forms an 'I'—an idealized, unified self it is not yet. On this view the ego is founded on a misrecognition, an image outside ourselves we then try to live up to, making the self inherently divided and alienated.
lacan-symbolic: Jacques Lacan divided human experience into three registers: the Imaginary (images and identifications), the Symbolic (the shared order of language, law, and social roles we are born into), and the Real (what resists symbolization altogether). On this view our sense of reality is structured by language, with an ungraspable remainder forever beyond it.
legal-positivism: Legal positivism is the view that whether something is law is a separate question from whether it is just. A rule can count as valid law because of who enacted it, even if it is deeply immoral—which, positivists argue, is exactly why we should say unjust laws are laws, but bad ones.
naturalistic-fallacy: The naturalistic fallacy is the mistake of arguing that something is good just because it is natural, or bad because it is unnatural. Related is David Hume's point that no 'ought' can be derived from an 'is': descriptions of what nature does do not by themselves yield moral conclusions about what we should do.
oedipus-complex: The Oedipus complex is Sigmund Freud's claim that young children pass through a phase of intense attachment to one parent and rivalry with the other, named for the Greek king who unknowingly killed his father and married his mother. Freud thought resolving it shapes adult personality; the theory is widely criticized today.
physicalism: Physicalism is the view that everything that exists—including minds, thoughts, and feelings—is ultimately physical, or depends entirely on arrangements of physical stuff. Many hold it follows that mental life just is brain activity; dualists disagree, arguing that consciousness or souls cannot be captured in physical terms. The debate tests what we think we are.
rectification-of-names: The rectification of names is a Confucian doctrine from the Analects: social order collapses when titles and realities drift apart, so a ruler must truly rule and a father truly father. Naming things rightly is a moral act—language aligns conduct, and hypocrisy begins with a title claimed but not lived.
schopenhauer-compassion: Arthur Schopenhauer grounded morality not in duty or consequences but in compassion: because we all share the same underlying reality, the suffering of another can strike us directly, and that pull is the true basis of justice and kindness. On his pessimistic picture, compassion is the rare spark that pierces ordinary self-interest.
stoic-premeditation: Premeditatio malorum—the premeditation of evils—is a Stoic exercise of regularly imagining misfortunes in advance: loss, failure, death. Practitioners like Seneca held this does not make us gloomy but prepared and grateful, stripping misfortune of its shock and teaching the difference between what we control and what we do not.
stoic-view-from-above: The view from above is a Stoic meditation, described by Marcus Aurelius, of mentally rising to look down on human affairs from a cosmic height—cities, quarrels, and ambitions shrinking to specks. On this view, seeing how small things are strips them of exaggerated importance and frees attention for what truly matters.
tabula-rasa: Tabula rasa—Latin for 'blank slate'—is John Locke's image of the mind at birth: empty of innate ideas, with all knowledge and character written by experience. The claim anchors empiricism and the nurture side of the nature–nurture debate, though many psychologists today hold we are born with innate capacities too.
wolf-meaning: Meaning in life is the question of what makes a life worth living for the person leading it, distinct from mere happiness or moral goodness. Susan Wolf's influential answer: meaning arises when 'subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness'—when we are actively and lovingly engaged with projects and people genuinely worth our devotion.
